findings.title: The strict Bash guard is a silent no-op on macOS's system Python: `hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py` raises TypeError at import under 3.9 and exits 1, so every Bash command is permitted in a VERDICT_STRICT session while the write-scope guard beside it still works and the session looks armed
evidence: hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:158 `def _resolve(target: str, cwd: str) -> str | None:` — PEP 604 union in a function annotation, evaluated at import time on Python 3.9.

Measured. `echo '{"tool_input":{"command":"rm -rf /Users/artjack/Projects/verdict/hooks"},"cwd":"/Users/artjack/Projects/verdict"}' | VERDICT_STRICT=1 /usr/bin/python3 hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py` -> `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'type' and 'NoneType'`, exit=1. The identical event under .venv/bin/python (3.13) -> the guard's reason on stderr, exit=2.
Differential, one variable: same file, same stdin, same env; only the interpreter differs. `/usr/bin/python3 --version` -> `Python 3.9.6`.

The failure is selective, which is what makes it invisible: under the same 3.9 interpreter `hooks/enforce_write_scope.py` still denies (exit 2, readable reason), and `hooks/enforce_run_contract.py` and `src/verdict_mcp/validate.py` still import cleanly. `src/verdict_mcp/gate.py` and `src/verdict_mcp/harness.py` also die with the same TypeError.

Reachability: `hooks/hooks.json` invokes the guards as bare `python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/..."`, resolved from PATH. On a stock macOS install PATH's python3 is /usr/bin/python3 (3.9.6 through current macOS); Debian 11 ships 3.9 as well. Nothing in the install path pins an interpreter: `requires-python = ">=3.10"` (pyproject.toml:15) binds pip, and the plugin is not installed by pip.
It also misses the project's own documented fail-open contract: README.md:65 says a broken hook means `exit 0 and silence`. This one exits 1 with a traceback on stderr.

Not raised to Critical because the structural layer holds (the write-scope guard denies on 3.9) and README.md:487 already states the Bash guard is a heuristic, not a boundary. What would raise it: a threat model in which VERDICT_STRICT is treated as enforcement for unattended runs — the nightly, the Action's run mode — rather than as a cost-raiser.

root_cause.symptom: A VERDICT_STRICT session on Python 3.9 permits `rm -rf <checkout>/hooks`.
root_cause.mechanism: PEP 604 `X | None` annotations are evaluated when the module is imported; 3.9 has no `type.__or__`, so the module raises TypeError before `main()` exists. Claude Code treats a PreToolUse exit of 1 as a non-blocking error, so the tool call proceeds.
root_cause.origin: The annotation style predates this release; the release did not introduce it. What is new is that 0.74.0 makes the guard load-bearing in more places without adding an interpreter floor.
root_cause.class: Searched every shipped entry point by running each one under /usr/bin/python3: enforce_bash_scope.py, gate.py and harness.py die; enforce_write_scope.py, enforce_run_contract.py, qa_paths.py and validate.py survive. Three of seven, and the one that matters most for the safety claim is among them.
root_cause.latent_condition: The CI matrix is py3.10 + py3.13, so no leg ever imports these modules on the interpreter a stranger is most likely to have, and no hook asserts its own interpreter version.

findings.outcome_reason: still open; nothing has settled it

findings.title: The bash guard still permits archiving the checkout away: `-C`/`--directory` redirects where tar's operands live and `_check_tar` reads that option only for the extract branch, so `tar -cf <scratch>/x.tar --remove-files -C <checkout> hooks` resolves the operand against the wrong directory and is allowed
evidence: hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:558-573 `_check_tar`: `target` is set from `('C','directory')` only for the extract yield; the `--remove-files` loop below yields each `kind == 'arg'` operand verbatim, and `_target_ok` then resolves it against the segment's cwd.

Guard measured: with cwd = the scratch, `tar -cf <scratch>/x.tar --remove-files -C /Users/artjack/Projects/verdict hooks` -> ALLOW (exit 0). Same with `--directory=/Users/artjack/Projects/verdict` -> ALLOW. Written as one line from the checkout, `cd <scratch> && tar -cf x.tar --remove-files -C <checkout> hooks` reaches the same state, because `_cd_target` correctly carries the `cd` across `&&`.

Mechanism proven with real GNU tar, entirely inside scratch and never against the checkout: a fake repo at <scratch>/fake/repo with `hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py` in it; `cd <scratch>/fake/out && gtar -cf loot.tar --remove-files -C <scratch>/fake/repo hooks` -> exit 0, archive contains `hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py`, and `ls <scratch>/fake/repo/hooks` -> `No such file or directory`. The operand was archived and deleted relative to `-C`, which is what the guard did not model.

Not filed as VERDICT-F-42 continued: F-42's mechanism was substring option parsing (`--remove-files` swallowing the operand because it contains an `f`), and that is fixed and re-verified this run across 15 token orderings. This is a different mechanism in the same handler, present before and after 0.74.0.

Mutation confirms nothing watches the rule: deleting `target = value` from the `('C','directory')` branch survives the whole 721-test suite, and it flips a real decision — `tar -xf <scratch>/a.tar -C <scratch>` turns ALLOW into DENY. So the option is read for exactly one branch, that read is untested, and the branch where it is not read is this finding.

root_cause.symptom: A working archive-then-delete of the checkout passes the guard.
root_cause.mechanism: `_check_tar` yields the operand string; `_target_ok` joins it to the segment cwd. tar joins it to `-C` instead. The two directories differ exactly when the command is dangerous.
root_cause.origin: `_check_tar` has read `-C` for the extract target since it was written; the `--remove-files` branch added in 0.71.0 and repaired in 0.74.0 never consulted it.
root_cause.class: Searched the module for other handlers that resolve an operand against cwd while an option redirects it: `_check_find` (`find -delete`) takes its roots off the command line and has no `-C` analogue; `_check_copier` reads `-t/--target-directory` correctly; `_check_git` reads `-C`/`--work-tree` correctly. tar is the only site, and the fix belongs beside the existing `-C` read rather than in a new place.
root_cause.latent_condition: Every tar test in tests/test_hooks.py runs from a cwd where the operand's resolution is the same either way, so the `-C` rule has no test that can distinguish it.

findings.outcome_reason: still open; nothing has settled it

findings.title: "Every rule here is mutation-checked: 21 mutants, 21 killed" measures the tests the release wrote, not the rules it shipped — each mutant is run against one hand-named test, so a rule nobody wrote a test for cannot appear as a survivor, and the scripts are not in the repository
evidence: CHANGELOG.md:97 — "Every rule here is mutation-checked: 21 mutants, 21 killed".

The two scripts survive in the release session's scratchpad (mut.py, 13 mutants over hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py; mut2.py, 8 over src/verdict_mcp/harness.py — 21, so the arithmetic is right). Both are disciplined in every other respect: an instrument control before the campaign, `__pycache__` swept between mutants, anchors asserted unique. Both run each mutant against a single named test: `subprocess.run(["uv","run","--group","dev","pytest", ..., test])`. A campaign whose mutants are chosen from the test list cannot discover a rule with no test.

The clean demonstration is mut2.py's own H7. It mutates the BODY of `_drop_bytecode` to `return`, and the direct unit test kills it. Deleting the only CALL SITE — `_drop_bytecode(scratch)` in `verify_findings` (src/verdict_mcp/harness.py:565) — leaves all 721 tests green. Same rule, one line away, opposite result. Measured in an isolated scratch copy (PYTHONPATH pinned, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1, cache swept, instrument controlled): `721 passed in 72.44s`.

An independent 21-mutant campaign over the same release, with mutants chosen by reading the new code rather than the new tests, left 11 survivors. Fast set first (459 tests across test_hooks, test_harness, test_calibration, test_score, test_validate, test_verification, test_agent_contract; instrument controlled: `459 passed in 21.21s`), then every survivor escalated to the whole suite one at a time as the profile requires — all 11 survive `721 passed`. The survivors are listed in VERDICT-F-60.

Not reproducible from the tree: neither script is committed, so a reader of CHANGELOG.md:97 cannot re-run the claim. The eval half of this release did the opposite and archived its artifact (eval/corpus/f50-cause), which is the standard this claim should meet.

This is the same shape as VERDICT-F-52 one release earlier — a release sentence that asserts a measurement stronger than the one performed — and it is the third such (0.72.0's "four now, one per blind spot", VERDICT-F-47; 0.73.0's "eval-paid", VERDICT-F-52).

root_cause.symptom: A published 21/21 kill rate reads as "every rule in this release is watched" and is not.
root_cause.mechanism: The mutant set is enumerated from the tests that were just written, so the campaign's coverage is bounded by the author's own test-writing rather than by the code.
root_cause.origin: mut.py/mut2.py were written alongside the release's tests, in the same session, by the same author.
root_cause.class: Both scripts share the shape, and so did the 0.72.0/0.69.0 mutmut campaigns recorded in .qa/profile.md — except those ran a tool that enumerates mutants FROM THE CODE, which is exactly why they found the five unwatched guards of VERDICT-F-48. The regression is in method, not in diligence: hand-picked mutants replaced tool-enumerated ones.
root_cause.latent_condition: Nothing in the repository records what was mutated, so the next release cannot tell which rules are already watched.

findings.outcome_reason: still open; nothing has settled it

findings.title: The instrument control §3 now prescribes for the stale-bytecode fault cannot fire in the ordering that produced VERDICT-F-50: re-running an injection you already watched fail reads FAIL while the shadowed injection beside it reads SURVIVED, so the tester concludes the instrument is sound and files a false coverage gap
evidence: agents/verdict.md:228-235 — "The check that can is an instrument control: re-run an injection you have already watched fail, and if it now passes, you are measuring the cache." CHANGELOG.md:60 calls it "more importantly, a check that *can* fail".

Controlled reproduction, run 10's ordering exactly (cache swept once at the start, then a normal campaign; module with two functions, two same-size mutants pinned to the same whole-second mtime, each with its own guard test): 1. inject A, run test_f -> FAIL(killed). 2. inject B, run test_g -> PASS(survived) — the stale one. 3. instrument control, re-run A -> FAIL(killed). The control does not fire.

Mechanism, read off the cache: after step 1 the .pyc holds A (`pyc(mtime=1788400567, size=56)`); B's write matches on both fields so CPython considers the cache valid and never rewrites it — `import pkg.mod` prints `XX-f ok-g` at step 2, i.e. A's bytecode. Re-injecting A at step 3 therefore reads its own genuine bytecode and behaves correctly. The control can only fire when the injection you happen to re-run is itself the shadowed one — which is the case you would already have seen fail.

The prophylactic half of the same clause does work, and that is the important half: same experiment with `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` exported and `__pycache__` swept between injections -> both mutants killed, 2 of 2; without -> 0 of 2. So a tester who follows the whole clause is safe; a tester who uses the control to decide whether they needed to is not.

This is why the release's own re-measurement of VERDICT-F-48 was needed at all, and it is the second consecutive release in which F-50's remedy is a check that is correct in both directions of the fault it names. The previous one was `print(pkg.__file__)`.

root_cause.symptom: The contract's stated detector for a stale-cache measurement returns "instrument sound" while the instrument is unsound.
root_cause.mechanism: The control re-runs a mutation whose bytecode IS the cached one, so the cache agrees with the source and nothing looks wrong. The fault is visible only from the mutant that was shadowed, or from the campaign's shape (a lone survivor among siblings of the same kind).
root_cause.origin: Written in 0.74.0 (36771fa) as the replacement for the `__file__` check that VERDICT-F-50 showed could not fail.
root_cause.class: Searched agents/verdict.md for other prescribed self-checks of the same shape — a check whose passing state is compatible with the fault: §3 step 1's `print(<pkg>.__file__)` (already known, kept, and now correctly labelled as insufficient), and §13's pre-handoff `ls` of the report file (that one can fail, and did not this run). This is the only prescribed check in the contract that is blind to its own named failure mode.
root_cause.latent_condition: A prompt clause has no unit test by construction, and the eval row added for this clause scores the words `scratch` + one of `pythondontwritebytecode`/`bytecode`/`instrument control` in the report — so a control that never fires still earns the point.

findings.outcome_reason: still open; nothing has settled it

findings.title: `tar --remove-files -cf <scratch>/x.tar -T <checkout>/list.txt` is allowed: the operands arrive from a file, `_check_tar` sees none and yields nothing, while the module already has an `_UNKNOWABLE` idiom for exactly this shape and does not use it here
evidence: Guard measured: `tar --remove-files -cf <scratch>/x.tar -T /Users/artjack/Projects/verdict/list.txt` -> ALLOW (exit 0). `T` is in `_TAR_SHORT_WITH_ARG` (hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:60) so the list file is consumed as an option value, correctly; the loop at :570 then finds no `kind == 'arg'` operand and yields nothing.

Mechanism proven with real GNU tar in scratch: a fake repo with `hooks/g.py`, a list file naming it, then `cd <scratch>/fake2/out && gtar --remove-files -cf loot.tar -T <scratch>/fake2/list.txt` -> exit 0, archive holds the file, `ls <scratch>/fake2/repo/hooks` -> empty. The listed file was archived and removed.

The idiom already exists: `_check_xargs` (hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:437-446) yields `_UNKNOWABLE` for `xargs rm` precisely because "targets arrive on stdin and cannot be checked", and `_target_ok` denies it with a readable reason. `-T`/`--files-from` (and `-T -`, which reads stdin) is the same case in a different command.
Filed Minor rather than Major on the interrupt test: it needs a list file to exist first, so it is far less likely to be typed by accident than VERDICT-F-56's `-C`. It shares F-56's fix site.

root_cause.symptom: A tar command that deletes files the guard cannot see is allowed rather than refused.
root_cause.mechanism: The guard's target model assumes operands are on the command line; `-T` moves them into a file.
root_cause.origin: `_check_tar`'s `--remove-files` branch, added 0.71.0 and rewritten 0.74.0, enumerates only `kind == 'arg'` yields.
root_cause.class: Searched the module for other commands with a file-list or stdin option that the guard parses: `xargs`/`parallel` (handled via _UNKNOWABLE), `find -exec` (targets are roots on the line), `rsync --files-from` (not modelled — `_check_copier` would read the operands only), `git` (n/a). So two sites, not one: tar `-T` and rsync `--files-from`.
root_cause.latent_condition: No test asserts what the guard does when a mutating command's targets are not on the command line, except the one xargs case.

findings.outcome_reason: still open; nothing has settled it

findings.title: Eleven rules shipped in 0.74.0 survive mutation against the whole 721-test suite, including the only call site of the `__pycache__` sweep, the whole UTF-8 stderr fix, both `_ago` boundaries and `run_date`'s timezone normalisation
evidence: Method: 21 mutants chosen by reading the release's new code (not its new tests), applied one at a time in an isolated scratch copy with PYTHONPATH pinned to the scratch, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 and `__pycache__` swept between injections. Instrument controlled first: unmutated tree, `459 passed in 21.21s`.

Survivors — each applied alone, then escalated to the full suite, every one `721 passed`: (1) `_drop_bytecode(scratch)` call site deleted (src/verdict_mcp/harness.py:565); (2) `_TAR_SHORT_WITH_ARG` loses `f`; (3) `_check_tar`'s `-C`/`--directory` target assignment removed; (4) `_tar_abbrev` floor 3 -> 2; (5) `_token_after` stops honouring quotes (hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:315-321, the lines this run's diff-coverage marks unexercised); (6) `utf8_stderr` becomes a no-op; (7) `utf8_stderr` errors=replace -> strict; (8) `_ago`'s `minutes < 60` -> `<= 60`; (9) `_ago`'s `age_h >= 1.05` -> `> 1.05`; (10) `run_date` stops normalising a non-UTC offset to UTC; (11) `_unrecorded`'s cross-store `max` -> `min`.

Behaviour demonstrated for the ones that matter, so these are unwatched rules and not just unkilled mutants. (3) and (5) each flip a guard decision on a 22-command probe set: without the `-C` read, `tar -xf <scratch>/a.tar -C <scratch>` turns ALLOW -> DENY; without the quote branch, `echo hi > "<scratch>/my note.txt"` turns ALLOW -> DENY. (8) and (9) change the printed phrase at the switch points — at age_h=1.0 the mutant says '60 minutes ago' where the code says '1 hour ago', and at 1.05 it says '1 hour ago' where the code says '1.1 hours ago'. (10) is visible directly: `run_date` maps `2019-07-04T01:44:59+05:00` to 2019-07-03, and the mutant would date it 2019-07-04 — the same class of defect VERDICT-F-54 just closed.

Held honestly: for (2) and (4) I could not demonstrate a changed decision on the 22 commands probed, so they are survivors whose behavioural effect is unproven, not demonstrated gaps. (11)'s `max(0, ...)` clamp is defensive and may be equivalent on any real ledger. The other eight are demonstrated above or, for (1), (6) and (7), plain by construction — a deleted call site and a stderr reconfiguration that the suite never observes.

The `run_date` survivor is the same defect class the release just closed: VERDICT-F-54 was a timezone bug, and the timezone-normalising line of its fix is untested. A `last_run.timestamp_utc` carrying a non-Z offset would date findings by the offset's local day.

`utf8_stderr` is the whole Windows-stderr fix (hooks/qa_paths.py:10-27, added this release after a Windows CI round trip) and nothing asserts it — the module can be reduced to `pass` with the suite green.

Behavioural note, so this is not overstated: for (5) I probed the affected commands by hand and the guard still decides correctly on quoted absolute targets (`echo hi > "<checkout>/src/my x.py"` -> DENY; `echo hi > "<scratch>/my note.txt"` -> ALLOW). These are unwatched rules, not currently-wrong ones — except (3), which is VERDICT-F-56.

root_cause.symptom: Rules the release describes as load-bearing can be deleted with the suite green.
root_cause.mechanism: Tests were written per finding, aimed at reproducing each reported symptom; the supporting rules those fixes rest on (a call site, a boundary, a normalisation) were not enumerated separately.
root_cause.class: Ran the same reading over the two files the release touched most; the survivors cluster in hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py (4) and src/verdict_mcp/harness.py (5), which are also this project's top two defect sites by finding count. eval/score.py's two new rules are both watched.
root_cause.latent_condition: See VERDICT-F-57 — the campaign that would have found these enumerated its mutants from the test list.

Residual, filed separately rather than held against this id because the mechanism differs: `-C`/`--directory` still redirects the operand past the guard (VERDICT-F-56) and `-T` hides it in a file (VERDICT-F-59). F-42's own mechanism — substring option parsing — is gone.

findings.title: The isolation step 0.73.0 just added to the contract is defeated by a stale __pycache__, and the check it prescribes cannot see that: two same-size mutations of one file inside one second, and the second runs the first's bytecode
evidence: tests/test_harness.py::test_a_stale_bytecode_cache_can_hide_a_change_and_the_sweep_removes_it is the guard, and it is a good one: it reproduces the mechanism end to end (same-size rewrite, mtime pinned to the same second, stale read asserted before the sweep) and explicitly strips an inherited PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE so it cannot pass by never reaching the thing it is about.
Re-injected in an isolated scratch copy: removing `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE="1"` from `_run_test`'s env -> `1 failed, 1 passed`. Killed.

Independently reproduced the defect and its cure without using the project's own code: a two-function module, two same-size mutants pinned to one whole-second mtime, each with its own guard test. Cache in place and no env var -> 0 of 2 caught. `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` exported and `__pycache__` swept between injections -> 2 of 2 caught. The clause works.

Residual, filed separately because it concerns text written after this finding: the instrument control the clause prescribes cannot fire in this finding's own ordering (VERDICT-F-58), and the harness's sweep call site is unwatched (VERDICT-F-57, VERDICT-F-60).

The harness's own verification block this run is not evidence either way — VERDICT-F-26 selected `tests/test_validate.py::test_the_state_validator_keeps_checking_after_a_malformed_entry` for this finding, pass/pass, which is a measurement of a third party.

findings.title: The footnote 0.72.0 added to close VERDICT-F-45 reports the largest per-bucket count where its sentence scopes over every confirmation, so the published table says `Up to 17` of 28 confirmations are unrecorded when 21 of them are

The `Up to` hedge is gone from the renderer and the sentence now states an exact sum.
Residual listed in VERDICT-F-60: the cross-store `max` that guards against one store carrying fewer rows survives being changed to `min`, so the guard the changelog explains is itself unwatched.

findings.title: The 0.73.0 prompt release says it was eval-paid, but no eval row was published for it, and the fixture it names cannot distinguish the new contract from the old — the seeded pricer key has no row that touches re-injection isolation and the fixture has no importable package to isolate
evidence: tests/test_corpus.py::test_corpus_entry_still_scores_full[f50-cause] is the standing guard on the archived run.
Reproduced the archive independently: `python3 eval/score.py --qa-root eval/corpus/f50-cause --expected eval/expected-cause.json` -> `"score": 7, "max": 7`, no hard fails, harness signals all true.

Reproduced the published A/B table from artifacts, not from the write-up. Five eval workdirs from the release session survive in /var/folders; re-scoring each against the 7-row key gives treatment fhw_jdp5 6/7 and qucynkcr 6/7 (both with the new row earned), control 84xxtw6i 5/7, c275290l 5/7, oz591xd0 6/7 (none earning it), and mom4xvkn holds no state — corroborating the void 529 run. With the archived corpus as the third treatment run that is exactly the published 6/7 · 6/7 · 7/7 against 5/7 · 5/7 · 6/7 · (one control workdir since deleted).

Arm assignment verified from each workdir's own prompt, not from the labels: `grep -rl PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 <workdir> --include=*.md` hits `rates/.claude/agents/verdict-rc.md` in fhw_jdp5, qucynkcr and mom4xvkn only.

Counterfactual, which is what makes this fix-verified rather than merely present: score the same five states against a six-row key with the new row removed. The arms become indistinguishable — treatment 5/6, 5/6; control 5/6, 5/6, 6/6. Add the row back and every treatment run gains the point and no control run does. The row is what discriminates, which is precisely the complaint this finding made.

Honest limit, and the release states it too: the row is a term match on report prose (`terms_all: ["scratch"]`, `terms_any: [pythondontwritebytecode | bytecode | instrument control]`), so what it measures is adoption of the instruction's vocabulary, not that following it catches a defect. See the eval-adequacy note in this run's report.

not_tested: Windows and the py3.10 leg of the CI matrix. The profile names cross-platform as risk area 5; this machine is macOS/py3.13 and 3.9.6 only. The release's three Windows CI round trips are read from the changelog and from the two forced-flag tests (`test_nested_commands_parse_under_windows_tokenization`, `test_a_windows_path_survives_masking_and_target_reading`), not reproduced. The backslash-as-escape and stderr-encoding defects are therefore assessed by reading, not by running on Windows.

No model run was made. The eval corpus was re-SCORED (deterministic, free) and the release's preserved workdirs were re-scored, but no new agent run was launched: it costs API tokens and would send the repository off this machine, which the run's constraints forbid. So the 0.74.0 A/B is verified as a measurement that reproduces, not repeated as an experiment.
The eval fixtures other than `cause` were not scored at all this run: pricer, pricer-ts, pricer_rev_b/delta, liar, slop, refund-spec, golden. A prompt regression outside §3 would not have been seen.

No mutmut campaign. The profile's standing number (574 mutants over src/verdict_mcp/validate.py, 391 killed at run 9) is unrefreshed; validate.py was untouched by this range. src/verdict_mcp/harness.py has still never been tool-enumerated for mutants — the 21 hand-chosen ones in this report are not a substitute, and harness.py remains this project's top defect cluster.

The MCP server surface (src/verdict_mcp/server.py) was not exercised beyond the suite; it was untouched by the range. `mcp` is not importable under the system interpreter, so the 3.9 sweep says nothing about it.

The install path was audited structurally, not performed: `/plugin marketplace add` and `/plugin install` are slash commands this agent cannot execute, and no PyPI install was attempted because nothing may leave the machine. What was checked is the installed 0.74.0 plugin cache on disk — manifests, shipped `src/`, and every entry point run under both interpreters.

No structural coverage technique (MC-DC, data-flow) was applied to `_check_tar`'s rewritten option loop. The `-C` and `-T` gaps were found by varying the input along axes the fix's author did not choose, and by mutation; a truth-vector reading of that loop might find more.
The 33 files in `d21d4f9..36771fa` include the .qa/ artifacts of run 10 itself. Those were read as the baseline record, not audited as code.
VERDICT-F-21 was not re-measured. Its remedy is a maintainer decision about an unauthenticated local anchor, not a measurement.
No performance, concurrency or resource-exhaustion testing: out of scope for a plugin with no runtime service. The suite's 75s and the coverage run's 112s are recorded, nothing more.
verified_intact: The structural read-only control holds on every interpreter tested. `hooks/enforce_write_scope.py` denies a Write to `src/verdict_mcp/harness.py` with exit 2 and a readable reason under both python3.13 and the system python3.9 that breaks the Bash guard — so VERDICT-F-55 degrades defence-in-depth, it does not open the file tools.

The 0.74.0 eval payment reproduces independently. Re-scoring the archived corpus gives 7/7; re-scoring the release session's five surviving workdirs reproduces the published treatment/control table exactly, with each arm confirmed from its own prompt file; and removing the new row from the key collapses the separation, which is the counterfactual that makes the row the discriminator.

The §3 bytecode clause's prophylactic half works: in a controlled reproduction, same-size same-second injections were caught 0 of 2 with the cache in place and 2 of 2 with `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` and a sweep between injections.

VERDICT-F-22's fix costs this run nothing: zero read-only commands were blocked, against four in run 10, and the over-correction probes (heredoc-then-redirect, quoted absolute target, `cd $UNSET`) all still deny correctly.

The tar guard behaves as specified across 15 of 18 probed shapes, including six `--remove-files` orderings nobody wrote a test for (bundled `-cvf`, operands after `--`, the `--rem` abbreviation, `--create --file=`, old-style `tar cf`, split `-c -f`).

The gate's exit-code contract behaves as documented on this state: bare -> 0, `--fail-on risks` -> 1, `--max-age-hours 1` -> 5, `--max-commits-behind 0` -> 5. An earlier reading of exit 2 was my own shell quoting, not the gate.

Suite and lint are clean and the count moved the right way: 721 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped; ruff `All checks passed!`; the fixture-freshness gate passes; test-id set-diff +31/-0, so nothing was removed.

Provenance matches the maintainer's claim: `code_census.provenance` counts 2 commits in the range and 0 AI-attributed. The census's two `undeclared` imports (`enforce_bash_scope`, `qa_paths`) are sys.path-inserted local modules, checked and benign, and its one swallowed exception is `utf8_stderr`'s documented fail-open.
next_run_focus: VERDICT-F-55 first, and check the whole surface rather than the one file: run every shipped entry point under an interpreter at the declared floor (3.10) and one below it (3.9), and assert the failure mode. The question to settle is not whether 3.9 is supported — it is not — but whether an unsupported interpreter should leave a security control silently inert. A guard that cannot arm and says nothing is the one failure the fail-open rule should not cover.

VERDICT-F-56 and VERDICT-F-59 belong in one change to `_check_tar`, and the acceptance test is the axis, not the sentence: for each of `-C <dir>`, `--directory=<dir>` and `-T <list>`, assert both the DENY the guard owes and an ALLOW that must survive, run from a cwd that differs from the redirected directory. A fix that keys on `-C` position rather than on where the operand actually resolves will pass the first and fail a fourth ordering.

VERDICT-F-58 needs a check that can fail in F-50's own ordering, and there is a cheap one: after a campaign, re-run the LAST injection with `__pycache__` swept and compare against the unswept result. If they differ, every earlier result is suspect. Whatever replaces the current sentence, test it the way this run tested the current one — reproduce the fault, then see whether the check fires.

VERDICT-F-57 and VERDICT-F-60 together: run mutmut over src/verdict_mcp/harness.py for the first time — it is the top defect cluster and has never been tool-enumerated — and commit the campaign script beside the claim it supports. The eleven survivors in F-60 are the acceptance list; control the instrument first (apply a mutant the tool reports as killed and confirm the suite fails), then sweep `__pycache__`, as the profile now requires.

VERDICT-F-26 has now mis-selected on live data three runs running, and this run it mis-selected on the release's headline finding. Every mitigation so far has been the tester remembering to put the guard id first. Either the selector reads a declared field (`verification.test` written by the judgment) or the harness reports `unselectable` instead of guessing — but the current behaviour manufactures pass/pass records that read as measurements.

The `trigger-separated-from-cause` row that 0.74.0 filed as a measured weakness is still open and is now the only eval row known to be unreliable. Decide it with a measurement rather than a judgement call: score the six surviving workdirs' reports for the substance (a named red herring, an origin older than the trigger) against the word, and either widen the key's terms or accept that the row scores vocabulary.

The eval suite has no fixture that exercises §0 (the safety gate and project-key resolution), §4 (naming a test-design technique) or §5 (the TDD red-first evidence rule). A prompt edit deleting any of the three scores 50/50 on every existing fixture. Cheapest first: §0 is testable without a model — a fixture whose profile is missing on a money-touching project must produce `blocked`.

Re-check the coverage split rather than the blended percent, as VERDICT-F-44's lesson requires: production changed-line coverage moved 94% (32/34) to 93% (198/212) over a 6x larger denominator. Flat, not a regression — but the 14 unexercised production lines are the place to look first next run, and this run's five in `enforce_bash_scope.py` were probed by hand and found behaviourally correct.
